quote: A cheap American imitation of Wagnerian hero worship. Neither operatic nor historically cognizant, Young Washington is nothing but cheap, uninspiring propaganda.
Stirring and inspirational without being preachy, Young Washington dramatizes the lesson that a brave man’s mistakes, when faced, can lead to his greatest triumphs.
It’s interesting and informative history, but not great filmmaking — the dialogue’s stilted, the acting at times is hyperbolic and the directional timing is off.
This one survives on strong performances and Erwin’s confident sense of place — not groundbreaking cinema, but a well-made piece of American cinematic history.
The movie is artistically conservative, with some of the bland sincerity of an afternoon special. Yet as afternoon specials go, “Young Washington” is a good one.
What the movie lacks is a clear moment when we collectively know that George is going to be the guy. A scene with real chills. In that sense it’s the viewer who feels ambushed… by disappointment.
This surface-level biopic pays a respectful, if not dull, nod to the first president of the United States.
Young Washington is unapologetically patriotic and occasionally idealized, but strong action, solid storytelling, and confident direction make it an engaging historical crowd-pleaser.

quote: The period accurate production design isn’t the film’s only surprise, as Franklyn-Miller gives an arresting performance as Washington.

Young Washington’s epic ambition clearly exceeded its limited grasp to realize its grand vision. It’s an earnest but cursory exploration of the first US President’s early years as a wannabe British officer in the French & Indian War.

As long as you’re not using it as source material for an exam, film hits a lot of broad strokes in a non-messy way and fulfills its obligation to tell a story specifically about a younger George Washington before things get more complicated.

Epic but nuance-free, one-dimensional story of the key developments in the early life and career that shaped the man before he became the monument. Few famous actors are ponderous anchors. Franklyn-Miller is appealing.

Instead or revealing how Washington really became the father of our country by way of speeches in the Continental Congress, the movie squeezes as much as it can out the plot to fashion an action movie using muskets and heavy cannon fire.
I liked the part where George Washington brandished double muskets and said "It's Washington Time!". This movie is about as accurate as a drunk truck driver at a men's urinal.
What better way to spend our nation’s 250th birthday than getting back in touch with America’s OG? So, forget about the Benjamins and go with the one on the One.

Aimed at a Christian demographic, the film plays like an ‘Afterschool Special’ with a hot Brit model acting the twentysomething rebel before he became our first POTUS. Sticks surprisingly close to history without finding a way to enliven it.
This film avoids controversy in favor of an old fashioned tale of leadership and patrotism at a time when our country could use a Hell of a lot more of both.
Young Washington offers a glimpse at romance, captures Washington’s passion for his homeland, and delivers a powerful message of overcoming the odds - it’s a history lesson worth indulging in.

By the time Washington is fighting the French in slow-mo gunfights, doing sick horseback stunts while sick with dysentery, any pretense that Jon Erwin’s film should be taken seriously is out the window.
Most of the characters are flat and the portrayals stagey.
Even if this movie feels like it more comfortably belongs on the History Channel instead of a wide summer break in theaters, it fills the bill for patriotism over this Fourth of July weekend.
Declamatory acting, cleanly stated motivations and a few solidly staged battle sequences are the order of the day.
Feeling much longer than its two hours, Young Washington suffers from the stiff, stodgy quality of so many historical dramas, especially those concerning that particular period of history.
Even apart from the dull filmmaking and hollow storytelling, the deeper complexities within the lens of Washington’s story are properly explored.
It's a story that is inherently compelling as a piece of overlooked history, but the execution of that storytelling is inherently flawed and counterintuitive.

The film demystifies Washington and shows him as simply a model American: hardscrabble, resilient, always learning and growing from setbacks. It’s interesting to see him come alive in this more relatable, not-yet-a-face-on-Rushmore way.
[It is] a well-crafted but accessible biopic about the maturation of a person who helped shape the nation’s image of itself.
Young Washington is a mediocre film hardly worthy of the Father of Our Country, George Washington.
Washington's ambitions and his strategic blunders in a skirmish with the French are the focus of this well-mounted but superficial biopic.

Kristopher Kimlin’s photography and David de Vos’ editing make the battle sequences work as they show the contrast between the gentlemanly style of fighting and the more chaotic approach that would become an American trademark.
OG POTUS gets a rip-roaring historical adventure chronicling his early days as an ambitious climber whose mistakes started a war and cost lives, but proved the forge to mold greatness.

Young Washington effectively portrays the sheer improbability of the free country that would follow this man’s unforgotten lead. It previews the unlikely triumphs -- and tragically regular loss of life -- it took to carve a land of imperfect liberty.

Young Washington is just competent enough to create that crisp tug of schoolkid patriotism the books we read as children provided. Nothing wrong with that, as long as you’re not an adult confusing feel-good heroism with the lessons of history.

Erwin’s most impressive achievements here are the battle sequences; between Kristopher Kimlin’s photography and David de Vos’ editing, they capture both the chaos of war and the specific fighting styles of the era.
A rip-roaring slice of rah-rah American history carved by war, wrapped in Sunday school homilies and served up as an Independence Day appetizer.
A movie marred by its flagrant over-acting and an abundance of tree-chopping references.
A mildly engaging, but somewhat dull biopic with great cinematography and set design.
Yet another semiquincentennial scam.

Washington learned from the many failures he endured, the mistakes he made. "Young Washington" provides a rousing example of one who learned from his experiences, rose from the ashes, and changed the world.

it will inspire you to learn more about Washington and other Founding Fathers. At the very least it’s a rousing reminder that even our greatest heroes start out as young men and women brimming with potential.
